body_markdown:
Phil Reilly was a 28-year-old engineer in 1963 at the Ford Research and Engineering Center in Dearborn, Michigan, when he ran across a nifty little sports car up for sale. The 1956 Porsche 356A Speedster 1600 Super, now considered a very impressive piece of German hardware, was just another small and, by American standards, underpowered foreign sports car with a limited but enthusiastic following. Nonetheless, Reilly was hooked.


Introduced to America in 1954 by Porsche at the insistence of[importer Max Hoffman](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/legendary-importer-max-hoffman-may-well-have-been-a-crook-but-were-all-in-his-debt/) , the Speedster experienced some success both in showrooms and on race tracks, but had largely run its course by ’63. And since Porsche’s 911 had just been introduced, a 356, even in Speedster form, was yesterday’s news, so Reilly was able to pick it up for just $1600, less than half of what it had sold for new and about 0.5% of what it is worth today.


Reilly still owns that Speedster, and it’s a beautiful machine, though Porsche aficionados will immediately notice where it departs from the norm. First, there is no handle on the front hood. It came with the car, but it wasn’t attached when Reilly bought it. The handle went on a shelf in his garage and there it has remained. “I like the look of the car better without the handle,” he said. Second, there are two grilles on the rear decklid. Other Speedsters of this vintage have only one. “I always liked the twin grilles of the 356B Super 90, so I installed a second grille on my 356A Sportster,” Reilly explained. Both front and rear views are attractive regardless of whether or not they alarm some purists. Reilly seems to relish that. He’s a man who knows what he likes and goes for it.


If the Reilly Porsche looks a little sleeker than the typical Speedster, it’s because the hood handle and badge were removed long ago, or perhaps never installed at the factory.


Paul Stenquist


The badging on the rear deck makes it known that this is a very special Porsche.


Paul Stenquist


Dual oval tailpipes exit under the rear bumper. With only minimal muffling, this car snarls.


Paul Stenquist


When Reilly purchased the car, it was finished in a pearlescent white, and the interior had been poorly upholstered in red vinyl. He’s repainted it twice. Today, the exterior is striking in a red finish that was used on some Porsche 944s. The tan interior that you see here was purchased from a supplier in Germany and is said to be similar to the original Speedster upholstery.


Reilly purchased this tan leather interior from a supplier in Germany, whose name has been lost to time. It was marketed as being very similar to the original with the addition of a few elegant touches.


Paul Stenquist


1956 Speedster 1600 Supers came with a three-gauge array behind the steering wheel. The speedometer and tachometer appear to be original. Reilly replaced a defective oil temperature gauge with the one seen here (center). He also installed an oil pressure gauge (hidden behind the steering wheel) and an ammeter.


Paul Stenquist


Like all Speedsters of this model and vintage, the car came from the factory with a 1600-cc engine equipped with a Hirth roller-bearing crankshaft. Way back in the 1960s, a friend of Reilly’s was racing Porsches and pined for a roller-bearing engine, like the one in Reilly’s car. So, they arranged a swap: a later-model Porsche 1600 engine with conventional bearings plus cash for the early roller-bearing engine. At the time, it was just a good financial deal for Reilly, but today it appears to have been an overall win. Porsche used roller-bearing cranks in early Super and Carrera engines because the longer stroke left no room for the standard connecting rods to clear the camshaft. In addition, it was thought that the roller bearings reduced friction and enabled a higher rev limit. But in practice, if oil flow was even slightly irregular, the rollers could flatten out on the crank and cause catastrophic engine failure, often pitching a rod through the crankcase. Over time, conventional bearing technology and motor oils advanced to the point where there was no friction advantage, and two-piece connecting rods solved the clearance problem. So, Porsche switched to conventional bearings for even their most powerful engines. Today, rebuilds of the early roller-bearing engines frequently include conversion to conventional bearings.


Reilly drove his Speedster for many years with the replacement 1600 engine, which was probably out of an early ‘60s 356. The engine has been rebuilt twice. In 2013, it was completely redone by Norris Racing Engines of Milford, Michigan. Norris installed new aluminum-finned cylinder barrels with 86-mm bores and new forged pistons, resulting in a displacement of 1719 cc. The crankshaft was modified for better oil flow. A Neutek street performance camshaft with 282° duration and .442-inch lift was mated with a three-angle valve job, blended ports, and new valve springs to help make the little boxer sing. A pair of 48 IDA Weber carbs hum right along. With over 100 horsepower on tap and a curb weight of about 1700 pounds, Reilly’s Speedster is a hoot to drive.


Reilly swapped the original engine, with its roller bearing crankshaft, for a later 1600-cc engine with conventional bearings. It’s been rebuilt twice, most recently in 2013 by Norris Racing Engines of Milford, Michigan.


Paul Stenquist


And drive it he has. For much of the ‘70s, the Speedster was Reilly’s daily driver, as he commuted from his home in Birmingham to Dearborn, a daily round trip of about 46 miles. Today, the car shows 87,000 miles on the clock, but with engine and transmission rebuilds, meticulous maintenance and regular replacement of wear parts like brakes, springs, shocks, bushings and more, it looks and runs as good as most low-mileage trailer queens. An engineer by trade, Reilly has done almost all of the work himself, and he continues to do so in his tenth decade.


Phil Reilly’s 1956 Porsche 356A Speedster 1600 Super outside one of his Michigan garages. The price on the pump is 33.9 per gallon—a little steep for 1956.


Paul Stenquist


I’m 13 years Reilly’s junior. On a visit to his garage—make that his three garages—I did all I could do to keep up. In truth, I couldn’t.


Speaking of those three garages, they’re far from empty. Residents include a Ferrari 308, a Ford GT, a ’48 Ford convertible with a Mustang drivetrain, a Shelby version of the first Fox-body Mustang, a T-bucket with 429 Ford power and matching trailer, and a Cobra replica built by Reilly with a full-race Ford 460 sporting four Webers, and of course the ’56 Porsche 356A 1600 Super Speedster. Oh wait, almost forgot: next to the T-Bucket is a big, black Harley with ape hangers and an extended fork. “I don’t ride much these days,” said Reilly. “I used to ride with a neighbor, but he moved away.”


The majority of Reilly’s machines were modified or built in the garages by this amazingly youthful nonagenarian, and they’re all driven and enjoyed. Why would they not be?


Reilly in one of his three garages with the T-bucket and trailer he built. Yep, that big black Harley with the ape hangers and extended fork belongs to this 91-year-old dynamo. He said he now rides it only occasionally.


Paul Stenquist


Garage number two houses a Ferrari 308 and an early Fox-body Shelby Mustang with just over 4000 miles on the clock. The third car is a family member’s daily driver.


Paul Stenquist


The Porsche lives in garage number 3 most of the time, along with a 460 cubic-inch Ford-powered Cobra replica that Reilly built, a Ford GT, and a chopped ‘48 Ford convertible in which Reilly installed a Mustang powertrain.


Paul Stenquist


Paul Stenquist


Paul Stenquist


The rear view of early Speedsters is appealing with the car’s smooth curves and small, round taillamps.


Paul Stenquist


The Speedster badging on the car’s flanks is timelessly elegant. Here, it catches pinpoints of sunlight.


Paul Stenquist


Paul Stenquist


Smooth hemispherical hubcaps on chrome steel wheels complement the Speedster’s soft curves. I don’t like seeing one of these cars with custom wheels, but some feel otherwise.


Paul Stenquist


The front hatch holds the fuel tank and a spare. Refueling required a deft touch to avoid spillage.
